w1.title: Worked Example 1: Electric Current, Potential Difference & Ohm's Law (V = IR)
w1.question: A 12 V solar battery is connected across a 4 Ω LED lamp resistor. Find the current.

steps.text: Given voltage V = 12 V and resistance R = 4 Ω.
Rearrange Ohm's Law: I = V ÷ R.

check.q: If resistance R is doubled while voltage V stays constant, what happens to the current I?

opts.m: Current I = V/R is inversely proportional to resistance.
Higher resistance reduces current flow for a fixed voltage.

w2.title: Worked Example 2: Series vs Parallel Resistor Networks
w2.question: Two 6 Ω solar classroom fans are wired in parallel. Find their equivalent resistance.

steps.text: Invert both sides to find Rp.
Equivalent resistance Rp = 3 Ω (less than either individual resistor).

check.q: Why are classroom lights and fans wired in parallel rather than series?

opts.t: Each appliance operates independently at full voltage
If one bulb fails, all other appliances turn off
opts.m: That is a drawback of series wiring, not parallel.
Parallel wiring reduces total equivalent resistance.

w3.title: Worked Example 3: Joule's Law of Heating (H = I²Rt) & Electric Power (P = VI)
w3.question: Find the power consumed by a 12 V, 2 A solar DC study lamp.

steps.text: Given potential difference V = 12 V and current I = 2 A.
Apply the electric power formula: P = V × I.

check.q: According to Joule's law H = I²Rt, if current I triples, heat produced becomes:

opts.m: Heat scales with I², so 3² = 9 times.
Heat increases with the square of current.

steps.title: Series vs Parallel Resistor Networks
steps.body: In series, total resistance adds up (Rs = R₁ + R₂). In parallel, reciprocals add (1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂) and each appliance gets full supply voltage.
